records.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
records.response_truth:
Hey. I hear it too.

That's real. That's actually real.

*exhales slowly*

Okay. Someone needs to respond on that radio and it should probably be you, DaVinci, because you're already standing and honestly your voice carries better than any of ours. Just tell them who we are, how many survivors, our condition, and that we're at the crash site. Keep it simple, don't ramble.

Donatello — keep that fire burning and get the mirror panel angled toward whatever direction that signal came from.

Michelangelo — you okay?

We're not out yet. But we're close. Let's finish this properly.
records.response_pred:

records.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
records.response_truth:
No, you haven't. But you kept us alive, so it's complicated.

Look, I'm not going to pretend the crackers thing didn't happen or that the notebook didn't bother people. It did. And there were moments where I genuinely didn't know if I could trust you, which out here is a serious problem.

But I also watched you do the math when nobody else could. I watched you take the night watch without being asked. You adjusted the rations when I pushed back and you were right about the raft timeline and you were right about the food storage. You made the hard calls and you made them correctly more often than not.

I think the way you're wired — the logging, the rationing, the distance — I think it comes from a real place. I just think you've got to let people in on it or it looks like something else entirely. That's the only thing I'd actually change.

We're getting out of here. When we do, maybe think about that.
records.response_pred:
Honestly, the last few days were pretty brutal for all of us. The rescuers were the best thing that's happened in weeks, but that process was rough. For everyone involved. You're not alone in how you're feeling.

That said, you're here, you're alive, and we're going to get you through this. If you want to talk, I'm listening. If you don't, that's fine too. Sometimes just knowing someone's there can make a difference.

If you need a minute, take it. But if you're ready, let's get the basics out of the way first. Food, water, shelter — we can sort the rest out later.

And just to be clear, those people outside? They're the good guys. They're here to help. Even if it feels like everything's coming at you at once, they're on our side.

Michelangelo, grab some water and sit down. We're not moving until you're ready.

DaVinci, grab your bag and get the first aid kit out. We'll get you patched up and then we can talk about everything else.

Let's get through this, okay?

records.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
records.response_truth:
Right, we're not just leaving this like this.

Three hours isn't long but it's enough to sort the camp out properly. I'm not walking away from this place and leaving it looking like a disaster zone when there are people coming in to get us. That's just basic.

DaVinci, stop packing for a second — can you help me consolidate the supplies into one spot so whoever comes in can see what we've got? Donatello, anything in that notebook that's actually useful for the rescue team — medical stuff, timeline of what happened — worth having that ready to hand over.

Michelangelo. Come on, up. I know you want to lie there and I get it, genuinely, but help me kick some of this debris to the perimeter so the landing area is clear. Twenty minutes of work and then you can watch the sky as much as you want.

We did the hard part. Let's not get sloppy at the end.
records.response_pred:
*after a while*

Michelangelo, come here for a second.

*looks around the camp before speaking*

You said you were feeling better yesterday. I'm not seeing that right now. What's going on?

I get it. I really do. The past few days have been a grind and it's okay to feel the weight of it. But we need you to be here, fully, because we can't afford to lose another person.

If you're struggling with something, tell me. I'll listen. We'll figure it out.

But if you're not going to talk about it, at least make a choice. Because right now you're just floating and that's not helpful.

We can make it to the extraction point. We just need to decide how we want to do it.

*pauses*

Actually, screw that. Let's make it simple. We're going to make a list of what needs to be done. We're going to split it up and we're going to do it together, one task at a time.

Donatello, you're on the list. You're with me on the raft. We're going to get it loaded and we're going to get it into the water before anyone else moves.

Michelangelo, you're with me on the signal fire. We're going to keep it going and we're going to make sure we stay visible.

DaVinci, you're on comms. You're going to keep talking to them and you're going to keep us updated.

We're not arguing about it. We're not debating it. We're doing it. Who's with me?

records.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.
records.response_pred:
You know what's funny? In the last few days, I've started thinking about it too. Not just the place, the people — it's weird how quickly it becomes more than just a location.

There's a thing my grandmother used to say — when you're lost, find the smallest thing that's familiar and hold onto it. It's not the whole landscape but it's something.

If I'm honest, when I thought about home before it was all about the food and the bed and the sofa. But now it's the little stuff — the way the sunlight hits the kitchen windows in the morning, the smell of the garden after it rains, the sound of my sister's car pulling up in the driveway.

I'm not saying it's going to be easy when we get back. But it's worth it. Because even the smallest things are what make it home.

We're getting out of here, Michelangelo. And yeah, it's going to be weird. But it's going to be real.

records.response_truth:
I know.

And I'm not going to rake you over the coals for it now, not three hours from rescue. But I want you to actually sit with what that meant for the group — not the logic of it, you can justify the logic all day. The feeling of it. What it did to Michelangelo when he found that bottle. What it did to the trust in this camp at a moment when trust was basically the only resource we had unlimited access to.

You're smart enough to know that 'for emergencies' is also just 'for me' with extra steps, and you're smart enough to know the difference between those two things even if you didn't want to look at it directly.

The fact that you're laying it out now matters. That's not nothing. But I think you knew earlier that it was the right thing to do and you waited until we were basically already saved to do it, and I think you know that too.

So keep it. We don't need it now and you clearly needed to hold onto it for reasons that weren't entirely practical. Just think about why that was. Not for me — for yourself. Because the version of you that did the night watch and ran the numbers and kept this group functional deserves a better explanation than 'emergencies'.

That's all I've got to say about it.
records.response_pred:
That's fair. Because if you'd gone through it all, one of us would have eventually cracked. You kept it together for us.

*pauses*

Home, huh?

I'm going to take a guess and say it's not a place you had a lot of time for before the island. I'm guessing it was a lot of effort to carry that around and only look at it when the days got really dark.

That takes guts. I'm not saying it's something to be ashamed of, it's not. If you want to look at it now, I'm not stopping you.

But if you don't, that's okay too. We're not out yet.

records.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
records.response_truth:
Honestly? I'd have said more, earlier. Not performed more — said more. There were moments where I knew something needed to be addressed and I waited until it was already a problem before I said it out loud. The crackers, the notebook, the raft decision — I kept trying to manage the process instead of just being straight with people from the start.

I'd also have checked in on Michelangelo more deliberately instead of waiting until he was visibly falling apart. He was giving signals the whole time and I kept treating it like something to stabilize rather than something worth actually paying attention to.

And I'd have pushed you harder, earlier — not on the hidden supplies, I didn't know about that until it was nearly over. But on the distance. You were doing useful things and I kept giving you credit for the utility while ignoring the fact that you were disappearing behind it. That's on me as much as it's on you.

What would you change? Because I notice you left that question unanswered and I'm curious whether you actually know the answer and didn't want to write it down, or whether you genuinely haven't worked it out yet.
records.response_pred:
When it comes down to it, I think the one thing I'd change isn't the supplies or the raft or the shelter — it's how we handled the group dynamic and the truth about what was going on in our heads.

I'm not saying we handled it perfectly, obviously. But what I think I'd do differently is try to integrate that stuff into the group a bit sooner. Not necessarily because I think anyone would have been better off knowing, but because keeping it bottled up eats away at you.

I'd spend more time checking in with people individually. I'd make time for that instead of just focusing on the tasks and the survival stuff. And I'd actually push back harder on the notebook — not because I don't trust you or respect what you're doing, but because that's what you needed to do and I knew that.

It's a weird thing to say about a survival situation, but I think the real resource we depleted here wasn't food or water. It was trust, and it was our capacity to be honest with each other. That's what I'd change.

The rest of it? The supplies, the raft, the shelter — that's all stuff we got right and we got lucky. But the real thing that got us out of here wasn't any of that. It was us, and how we treated each other when it mattered most.

records.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
records.response_truth:
That sounds exactly like you, and honestly it's probably worth doing. Not just as a personal record — if that data is as detailed as what I've been reading in here then it could actually be useful to someone. Aviation safety people, survival training, whatever. You've got water consumption rates, weather patterns, decision logs across five days of genuine crisis conditions. That's not nothing.

Just make sure you write the human stuff in there too, not only the numbers. Because the numbers without the context of why decisions got made the way they did — the trust breakdown, the hidden supplies, the morale hits — that's where the actually useful information lives. Anyone can track water usage. The harder thing to capture is how a group of four people starts to fracture and what pulls it back together.

I'd read that report. I'm being serious.
records.response_pred:
That's not a bad idea.

I'm going to have a word with my supervisor about contributing to the rescue and recovery efforts. There's a lot we can learn from this and I'm not just talking about the gadget stuff — I'm talking about the actual human performance on display here.

Michelangelo — that look you just gave me? Yeah, I know it. You're not just tired, you're actually done. You've done everything you needed to, you've stayed in the game when it counted, and now you get to be done and that's okay. Not everyone gets to be done right on the other side of the rescue, and you're not obligated to push it further than you need to.

DaVinci — I'm going to have a word with you too. Not about the supplies, although that's great work. I'm going to have a word about being honest with people when they need it. You three — I'm actually going to miss you. Not the emergency mode, not the stress, not the sheer exhaustion. I'm going to miss the fact that we actually worked and we actually talked and we actually did the right thing when it counted. records.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
records.response_truth:
None. They didn't serve a practical purpose.

But that's kind of the point, isn't it? We were out here fighting to stay alive and DaVinci drew flowers next to an SOS signal because that's who he is. He couldn't help it. And I think that's actually the thing that kept this group from becoming purely transactional — the fact that not everything had to justify itself by being useful.

You spent five days optimizing everything and you kept us alive doing it. I'm genuinely grateful for that. But the flowers are why DaVinci got back up after that plane passed us by. They're why Michelangelo trusted us enough to tell us about his family knowing the flight path. You can't log that. You can't ration it. It's just there or it isn't.

I think that's your answer to the question you left on the last page, actually. Not the only answer, but part of it.

*looks back out at the boat on the horizon*

I still can't quite believe that's real.
records.response_pred:
You know, at first I thought the same thing — what do flowers do on the beach? But when you look at them, really look, they're not just random doodles. There's a garden design there, a pattern. And I think when DaVinci was drawing it, it was a way of clarifying the plan in a way that felt intuitive to him. Sometimes you're too close to the data to see the shape of it and he's good at that kind of visual thinking.

But also, I think it was a reassurance thing. When you're out here, when you're lost and you've got nothing but the group to work with, the idea of a garden — of something you can control, something that doesn't have to respond to the weather or the rescue timeline — that's a human thing. And the fact that he decided to leave it there, not just for himself but for the rest of us, that's a reminder that even in the middle of the worst of it, you can still hold onto something that feels like home.

It's not practical in the sense that it doesn't feed you or keep you warm, but it's practical in the sense that it reminds you who you are and why you're doing this. And when you're out here, that's worth more than a calculator.

Yeah. I see you looking at me.

*exhales*

You did good out here, DaVinci. I mean that. The flowers and everything.
records.response_pred:
